newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein leaders urge end of hijackings, riots.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein leaders urge end of hijackings, riots.

text.p: The leaders of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, called on Catholic youths on Monday to stop car hijackings and burnings that erupted in protest at the holding of a Protestant parade.
Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams and his chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, made the appeals separately after one of the worst nights of violence in Northern Ireland for years.
"We want to call for an end to the hijackings and burnings," Adams told a Belfast news conference as the hulks of hijacked vehicles smouldered in nearby streets.
Their appeals were the first public attempt by Sinn Fein for calm since the province began counting down to the climax of the Protestant marching season next Sunday.
Across the province Catholic youths used the well-worn tactic of hijacking cars, setting them alight and then stoning or throwing petrol bombs at emergency services and police.
In the border town of Newry alone 221 vehicles were hijacked in 36 hours, police figures showed.
Adams, whose party shares the Irish Republican Army's goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland, called for "calm and dignified protest."
He made no mention of IRA sniper attacks on British security forces which took place during the night in one of the biggest displays of IRA firepower for years.
The IRA and a breakaway group, the Irish National Liberation Army, fired dozens of shots at security forces overnight. A policewoman was injured in the face, but not seriously.
Sinn Fein says it is a separate organisation from the IRA which shares the same goals. Its pro-British Unionist foes and many security officials say the two organisations overlap.

McGuinness, who issued an appeal to Irish nationalists on Sunday to "take to the streets" in protest, said in a statement that the "anger and frustration of nationalists in Northern Ireland is understandable."
But he added: "The riots and damage to property is counter productive."
McGuinness accused the Royal Ulster Constabulary Police of "disgraceful behaviour" in sealing off the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown on Sunday to allow an Orange Order march past.

"The British government and sections of the media will manipulate the scenes of disorder to disguise its culpability for the disgraceful behaviour of the RUC and the British Army on the Garvaghy Road yesterday morning," his statement said.
On Saturday night McGuinness told a huge rally in the Irish nationalist stronghold of Londonderry that Roman Catholics were like "the people of Chile, Nicaragua, El Salvador and South Africa.
"The place to be demanding justice is on the streets confronting your opponents," he said.
Northern Ireland's security forces logged the following tally of violence since Saturday evening, the eve of the fateful march:
-- more than 1,600 plastic bullets were fired in 36 hours;
-- there were 500 attacks on security forces;
-- 691 petrol bombs were thrown;
-- 80 people were injured, 34 civilians and 46 police;
-- 41 people were arrested.
